description.summary: Reported deaths in which a human body is severely burned, often reduced to ash, with little damage to the surroundings and no obvious external ignition source. Modern forensic science treats these cases as conventional fires propagated by the 'wick effect'.
description.full: Spontaneous human combustion (SHC) is the popular name for a small set of reported death cases in which a body is severely or almost completely consumed by fire — frequently leaving the torso reduced to ash while the extremities and the immediate surroundings show comparatively little fire damage. The classic case profile, first noted in early 19th-century medical literature, describes an elderly, often alcoholic, often immobile victim found alone near a fireplace, candle, or smoking material. Mainstream forensic science, supported by experimental work and case-by-case review, attributes such deaths to the 'wick effect': a small external ignition source chars clothing and skin, releases subcutaneous body fat, and the fat-soaked clothing burns slowly like a candle wick for many hours, locally consuming the body while the temperature elsewhere in the room remains low. Investigators including Joe Nickell and John F. Fischer have argued that an external ignition source is identifiable in essentially every well-documented case once the published account is checked against the forensic record. SHC nonetheless retains a strong cultural footprint, anchored by Charles Dickens's depiction of Mr. Krook's death in Bleak House (1852–53) and a small number of widely-reprinted cases from the 18th to the 21st century.

etymology.origin: First proposed in English by Paul Rolli, FRS, in a 1746 article in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society describing the death of Countess Cornelia Bandi of Cesena.
etymology.meaning: 'Spontaneous' (from a body's own internal cause, without external ignition) combined with 'human combustion'.

related_phenomena.name: Wick effect
related_phenomena.description: Forensic mechanism by which clothing and body fat sustain a slow body fire from a small external ignition source

related_phenomena.name: Pyrokinesis
related_phenomena.description: Alleged psychic ability to ignite fires; sometimes invoked by paranormal theorists for SHC

features.description: Trunk often reduced largely to ash, including bone, in cases where surrounding combustibles are barely scorched
Lower legs, feet, and hands are frequently found relatively undamaged
Damage to the room is often limited to a halo of soot above the body and melting of nearby plastics or fabrics
An oily, yellow-brown residue is frequently deposited on walls and ceiling near the victim

physical.morphology: The post-mortem state is described in forensic literature as consistent with prolonged, low-temperature smouldering combustion of the body fueled by the victim's own fat through clothing acting as a wick.

habitat_preference: domestic indoor settings (armchairs, beds, near hearths)
patterns: Victim typically elderly and living alone
Often a heavy smoker or with smoking materials nearby
Frequent association with alcohol consumption or reduced mobility
Most cases occur indoors with a small ignition source close at hand

range.description: Reported cases cluster in Europe (especially Britain, Ireland, France, Italy, Germany) and North America from the 17th century onward; isolated cases elsewhere.

first_recorded.source: Death of Countess Cornelia Bandi, Cesena, Italy (later reported in Rolli, 1746, Phil. Trans.)

peak_activity_periods.description: Victorian medical and literary interest; SHC associated with chronic alcoholism in physician treatises
Post-Reeser revival of public interest; foundational forensic re-examinations published

origins.cultural_roots: Emerged from 18th-century European medical case literature attempting to classify unusual death scenes; reinforced in Victorian medicine by treatises associating heavy drinking with body flammability.
origins.earliest_accounts: Paul Rolli's 1746 paper to the Royal Society on the 1731 death of Countess Cornelia Bandi is generally cited as the first scholarly account in English.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader European folkloric beliefs that vice, particularly drunkenness, could manifest as a literal inner fire.

timeline.event: Countess Cornelia Zangari Bandi found dead in Cesena, Italy, partly reduced to ashes; the case is later treated as the prototypical SHC report
timeline.source: Rolli, P. (1746), Phil. Trans. R. Soc.

timeline.event: Paul Rolli publishes 'A Letter ... concerning the Death of the Countess Cornelia Zangari & Bandi' in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society
timeline.significance: First English-language scientific paper on the phenomenon

timeline.event: Charles Dickens publishes Bleak House in book form; the death of the rag-and-bone dealer Mr. Krook by spontaneous combustion is publicly defended by Dickens against critics including G. H. Lewes
timeline.significance: Anchors SHC firmly in popular Victorian imagination

timeline.event: Death of Mary Reeser in St. Petersburg, Florida, USA; her body is found largely consumed in an armchair
timeline.significance: The most-cited 20th-century case; FBI investigation rejects SHC and points to a dropped cigarette

timeline.event: Joe Nickell and John F. Fischer publish a multi-part forensic survey of 30 alleged SHC cases (1725–1982) in Skeptical Inquirer / The Fire and Arson Investigator
timeline.significance: Argues that all reviewed cases have plausible external ignition sources
timeline.source: Nickell & Fischer, Fire and Arson Investigator (1984)

timeline.event: Michael Faherty, age 76, dies in his home in Ballybane, County Galway, Ireland; in 2011 coroner Ciaran McLoughlin records 'spontaneous combustion' as cause of death
timeline.significance: First case in modern times in which a coroner's verdict explicitly used the term SHC

history.modern_era: Mainstream forensic science treats SHC as a folk explanation. Experimental work (e.g. the 1998 BBC Q.E.D. wick-effect demonstration with a clothed pig carcass) has reproduced the characteristic burn pattern and limited room damage, supporting a conventional fire-dynamics explanation.

notable.name: Death of Countess Cornelia Bandi
notable.description: The 62-year-old countess was found in the morning by her maid as a heap of ashes on the bedroom floor with her legs, intact in stockings, and skull lying nearby. Surrounding furnishings were largely undamaged. The case was investigated and reported in Latin by Giuseppe Bianchini, then translated into English by Paul Rolli in 1746.

credibility.notes: Foundational European case for the SHC literature.

sources: Rolli, P. (1746), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 43

notable.name: Mary Reeser case
notable.description: Mary Reeser, 67, was found the morning after taking sleeping pills and smoking a cigarette in her armchair. The chair, Reeser's torso, and one slipper-clad foot remained; the rest of her body was reduced to ash. The FBI investigation concluded a dropped cigarette ignited her clothing, with body fat sustaining combustion through the wick effect.

notable.name: Michael Faherty case
notable.description: Faherty, 76, was found burned in his living room in front of an open fireplace; the fire damage was confined to his body and a small area of floor and ceiling above him. After investigation, West Galway coroner Ciaran McLoughlin returned a verdict of 'death by spontaneous combustion' in September 2011, the first such verdict in modern Irish or British inquest records.

factors: Coroner used the SHC label despite that ignition source
credibility.notes: Frequently cited by both proponents and skeptics.

physical.name: Mary Reeser remains
physical.description: Skull, vertebra fragment, foot in slipper, and a quantity of greasy ash in a charred armchair, photographed and catalogued by St. Petersburg police and the FBI.
physical.analysis: FBI laboratory concluded the burning was consistent with prolonged, low-temperature combustion fueled by body fat after ignition by a dropped cigarette.

photographic.name: Reeser scene photographs
photographic.description: Crime-scene and forensic photographs of the Reeser apartment, widely reprinted in subsequent SHC literature.

documentary.name: Rolli letter to the Royal Society
documentary.description: Paul Rolli's translated and annotated letter on the death of Countess Bandi, published in Philosophical Transactions.

documentary.name: Nickell and Fischer SHC case survey
documentary.description: Multi-part forensic re-analysis of 30 historical SHC cases between 1725 and 1982.
documentary.analysis: Concluded that an external ignition source is identifiable in essentially all reviewed cases.
documentary.source: Nickell & Fischer, Fire and Arson Investigator (1984)

paranormal.name: Pyrokinesis / poltergeist hypothesis
paranormal.description: SHC reflects an unexplained internal or psychic ignition mechanism, sometimes linked to poltergeist phenomena.
evidence_cited: Apparent absence of an external flame in some accounts
Anecdotal co-occurrence of unexplained domestic fires

scientific.name: Wick effect
scientific.description: A small external flame ignites clothing, which chars and splits the skin, releasing subcutaneous fat that soaks the cloth and burns at low temperature for hours, consuming the body while leaving the room largely intact.
evidence_cited: Reproduction of greasy soot deposition pattern

scientific.name: Acetone / ketosis hypothesis
scientific.description: Severe alcoholism or starvation produces elevated blood acetone, in principle slightly lowering ignition temperature; suggested as a contributing factor rather than a cause.
evidence_cited: Documented elevated acetone in alcoholic ketoacidosis

skeptical.name: Conventional fire with omitted ignition source
skeptical.description: Reported SHC cases are conventional house or armchair fires whose ignition source (cigarette, hearth ember, candle, electric heater) is either lost in the burn or omitted from the published narrative.
evidence_cited: Case-by-case re-investigation showing ignition sources in original reports
Low room temperatures consistent with smouldering rather than flash combustion
Pattern of elderly, immobile, and intoxicated victims near sources of fire

stories: Mr. Krook's death in Dickens's Bleak House
folklore.beliefs: In Victorian Britain, SHC was widely understood as a moral consequence of heavy drinking; this interpretation underwrites Dickens's use of the device against the rag-and-bone dealer Mr. Krook.

literature: Dead Souls — Nikolai Gogol (1842, the death of the landowner Korobochka's drunk peasant)
film_tv: This Is Spinal Tap (1984) — running gag about exploding drummers
other: Frequent feature article in tabloid and 'unexplained' magazine series of the 1970s–80s (Fortean Times, etc.)

researchers.name: Paul Rolli, FRS
researchers.contribution: First English-language scientific paper on alleged SHC

researchers.name: Joe Nickell
researchers.contribution: Forensic case review and skeptical analysis of SHC literature

researchers.name: John F. Fischer
researchers.contribution: Co-author of the 1984 multi-case SHC survey with Nickell

researchers.name: John de Haan
researchers.contribution: Experimental fire-dynamics work on the wick effect with clothed pig carcasses

organizations.name: Committee for Skeptical Inquiry
organizations.focus: Skeptical investigation of paranormal claims, including long-running SHC coverage

research.ongoing_studies: No active scientific research programmes treat SHC as a real anomaly; ongoing forensic interest concerns refining the understanding of the wick effect and other low-temperature body-fire dynamics.
